# Livarix

> An independently published guide to Livarix, a liver support dietary supplement sold as 60 capsules per bottle, two capsules daily. Written for readers in the United States at https://livarix.vercel.app/. Orders complete on the seller's own checkout. Last reviewed 15 November 2026.

Livarix publishes a milligram dose for every ingredient rather than hiding them inside a proprietary blend. The eight published ingredients are turmeric root powder 300 mg, beet root powder 200 mg, dandelion leaf powder 100 mg, artichoke extract 50 mg standardised to 5% cynarin, ginger root powder 50 mg, milk thistle powder 50 mg, alfalfa leaf powder 20 mg and L-cysteine HCl 10 mg, totalling 780 mg. The seller's suggested use is two capsules daily with a large glass of water, preferably in the morning with food, making one bottle a 30-day supply. The product is described as non-GMO, free of stimulants and made in the USA. Packs are $79, $69 and $49 per bottle for two, three and six bottles; only the six-bottle pack has free US shipping and three bonus digital guides. Every pack has a 60-day money-back guarantee. No published trial has tested the finished formula, and liver conditions need medical diagnosis and care. Sold to adults 18 and over.

## Sources cited on this page

- [NIH LiverTox: turmeric](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548561/): identifies turmeric as the most common cause of clinically apparent herbal liver injury in the United States, at an incidence of roughly 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000.
- [NIH LiverTox: milk thistle](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK548817/): human evidence described as promising but unproven, and milk thistle itself rated unlikely to cause liver injury.
- [NIDDK: definition and facts of NAFLD and NASH](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/liver-disease/nafld-nash/definition-facts): what fatty liver disease and NASH are, in plain language.
- [MedlinePlus: liver diseases](https://medlineplus.gov/liverdiseases.html): consumer background on liver conditions, symptoms and tests from the National Library of Medicine.
- [FDA: dietary supplements](https://www.fda.gov/food/dietary-supplements): how supplements are regulated as food rather than as medicine in the United States.
- [FTC: health claims](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/advertising-marketing/health-claims): the advertising rules covering health claims and endorsement disclosure.
